newsitem.title: TAIWAN: FEATURE-Taiwan loath to let HK chart its future.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Taiwan loath to let HK chart its future.

text.p: For the estranged Republic of China on Taiwan, Hong Kong's return to Chinese rule redraws the battle lines in an epic Taipei-Beijing rivalry, with Taiwan's dignity -- and business worth billions -- at stake.

Hong Kong's British status, Chinese pedigree and easy proximity has enabled it to straddle the duelling Chinas as a neutral middleman since their 1949 civil war split, earning huge profits and access to both markets in the process.
Taiwan and China have benefited, too.

During its two-decade-old reform era, communist China has used Hong Kong as a gateway through which to woo US$30 billion in Taiwan investment along with the Taiwanese industrial and business acumen that flowed in on the tide of capital.

Taiwan, too rich to sustain the cheap export manufacturing that made it an "Asian dragon", has made Hong Kong a buffer zone through which to tap China's vast labour pool, resources and markets without having to deal directly with Beijing.

Taiwan's big fear is that Hong Kong's shift into Beijing's camp will undermine this commercial symbiosis -- turning Hong Kong into a lever with which Beijing can squeeze what it sees as a renegade province into final submission.
"We know they will try to exact some concessions from us, but how far will they go? We just don't know," said China-watcher Shaw Yu-ming, a former government spokesman.
REJECTING "ONE-COUNTRY, TWO SYSTEMS"

Taipei dismisses any link between Hong Kong's future and its own, rejecting what Beijing sees as a generous offer: political, economic and even military autonomy under a "one country, two systems" deal now being pioneered in Hong Kong.

Taiwan "cannot accept the 'one country, two systems' formula imposed on Hong Kong by Peking because the state of division across the Taiwan strait differs categorically from Hong Kong's situation", President Lee Teng-hui wrote recently.
Despite their economic interdependence, Taiwan and Hong Kong have diverged politically since 1984, when Deng Xiaoping and Margaret Thatcher endorsed Hong Kong's 1997 return.

Hong Kong has tied its fortunes to China's economic boom, but has seen its democratic aspirations thwarted by Beijing. Its handover at midnight on June 30 will herald cautious steps toward a communist-vetted pluralism, much to the dismay of local democrats.

By contrast, Taiwan has shed its authoritarianism to embrace the stuff of Hong Kong democrats' dreams: universal suffrage and directly elected government, from lowly town councils to the rough-and-tumble parliament -- even the presidency.

Taiwan, the Nationalist republic's last redoubt after its 1949 defeat by the communists on the mainland, lifted martial law in 1987 and ranks among Asia's most liberal societies, growing ever more estranged from China's tight social controls.
CHINA SEEN PLAYING A RISKY GAME

As the political breech widens, experts say China is playing a risky game by freezing even informal contacts with Taipei and menacing it militarily, as it did with massive sustained war games and missile tests near the island in 1995-96.
"If you lose those linkages, then you lose Taiwan," said Taipei strategic analyst Andrew Yang.
An increasingly leery Taiwan has sought to cool investors' China lust, banning major infrastructure investments and trying to nudge capital toward Taiwan projects or Southeast Asia.
Yang predicted Beijing would sweeten investment incentives in hopes of keeping Taiwan engaged, but said China's communists underestimate the island's democratic impulses.
Most alarming to China, Yang said, was not Taiwan's elections so much as pending moves to amend the constitution to legalise popular referendums -- the key to self-determination.
"If you have a plebiscite or referendum, you can decide anything by a vote -- even change the name of the country, the flag, everything," he said.

Taiwan says it no longer can make backroom deals as it might have done before its political renaissance, and scorned mainland President Jiang Zemin's offer to name a Taiwan official as his vice president after reunification.
"We are a democracy. The government cannot go against the will of the people," Lin Chong-pin, a vice chairman of the cabinet's Mainland Affairs Council, told Reuters recently.
BEIJING SAYS INDEPENDENCE IS NO OPTION
Beijing vows to turn its three million-strong People's Liberation Army on Taiwan to thwart any independence play.
With such threats in mind, Taipei doubts China's assurances that all will be business as usual in Hong Kong, expecting that Beijing will use the territory to strongarm Taiwan.
The squeeze is already well under way.

A year ago, Taipei and Beijing reached indirect agreement on air links to Hong Kong. In exchange for keeping its airlines' existing Hong Kong routes, Taiwan was forced to open its market to two carriers controlled by mainland interests.

In indirect talks over the future of huge Taiwan-Hong Kong shipping flows, Beijing put sovereignty above trade, refusing to allow ships flying the Republic of China flag to enter Hong Kong harbour. At the 11th hour, Taiwan accepted the terms.
China also has used Hong Kong to sweet-talk Taiwan.

The official Xinhua news agency said Taiwan, a diplomatic pariah recognised by just 30 countries, should delight at the prospect of Hong Kong-style reunification with its promise of "international respect and glory".
For now, analysts say the safest money is on preservation of the status quo through the handover and probably long after.
Beijing, loath to imperil its economic ties with Taiwan or Hong Kong, has signalled a willingness to leave well enough alone until the 21st century as long as Taiwan checks its diplomatic ambition.
